title: Red, green, refactor
summary: The TDD loop in small steps: a test list, a failing test, the least code that passes, then cleaning up with the tests green. Replayed on the string calculator kata, then done by you.

steps.title: The loop
body: Test-driven development (Kent Beck) is a short loop, repeated every few minutes:
1. **Red**: write one small test for the next bit of behaviour, and watch it fail. Seeing it fail proves the test can fail, and that it tests the thing you think.
2. **Green**: write the **least** code that makes it pass. Hard-coding a value is allowed ("fake it"); the next test will force the real logic ("triangulate").
3. **Refactor**: with every test green, clean up names, duplication and structure. The tests are your safety net; behaviour must not change.
Before you start, write a **test list**: the cases you can think of, smallest first. Cross them off; add new ones as you discover them.

Why bother? The design comes from *using* the code first, every line exists because a test needed it, and you always know the last change that broke something: it was two minutes ago. TDD is not about testing; it is a way of writing code in small, safe steps.
Step through a real session on the **string calculator** kata (`Add("1,2")` is 3):

testviz.title: String calculator, one test at a time

code: public static int Add(string numbers) => throw new NotImplementedException();
steps.note: The first test is the simplest case on the list. It fails with `NotImplementedException`: red, for the right reason.
**Fake it.** Returning `0` is the least code that passes. It feels silly, and that is the point: the test, not your guess, decides what code exists.

code: public void One_number_is_itself(string input, int expected)
steps.note: **Triangulate.** Two examples make the fake impossible: no constant returns both 4 and 17.
The simplest real logic for the cases so far. Run all tests, not only the new one.
Fails with a `FormatException` from `int.Parse("1,2")`. Read the failure: it tells you what to build next.
**Obvious implementation.** When the right code is obvious, write it. `Split` + `Sum` also covers "any amount", so that item is crossed off for free (add a test to prove it).
Green, so now tidy: a named list of separators makes the next requirement (newlines) a one-word change. Refactor only on green, and run the tests after each small move.

steps.prompt: Put one TDD cycle in order.
lines: Pick the next case from the test list
Write a test for it and run it: it fails
Write the least code that makes it pass
Clean up the code and the test, running the tests after each change
steps.explain: Red, green, refactor. Watching the new test fail first is not optional: a test that has never failed may be testing nothing.

steps.prompt: You wrote a new test and it passes immediately, before you changed any code. What should you do?
options: Be suspicious: check that the test can fail (break the code briefly, or check it calls what you think), or accept that the behaviour already existed and pick the next case
Celebrate and move on: green is the goal
Delete the test because it adds no value
Make the test more complicated until it fails
steps.explain: A test that never went red has not proven it can detect anything. Often it is fine (an earlier step already covered the case); sometimes it asserts on the wrong thing. Ten seconds of breaking the code tells you which.

steps.prompt: Match each TDD move to its meaning.
pairs: return a constant to get to green quickly
add a second example so the fake no longer works
write the real code when it is clear
the cases still to do, smallest first
change structure with all tests green, behaviour unchanged

steps.title: Kata: the string calculator
prompt: Test-drive `public static class StringCalculator` with `public static int Add(string numbers)`. Work down the list, one test at a time, red first:
3. A custom separator can be declared on a first line: `"//;\n1;2"` is `3`.
4. Negative numbers throw `ArgumentException` with the message `negatives not allowed: -2, -4` (every negative, in order).
5. Numbers above 1000 are ignored: `"2,1001"` is `2`, but `"1000,1"` is `1001`.

Write your own `public class StringCalculatorTests` as you go: at least **6** tests (each `[InlineData]` row counts). **Run checks** runs your tests and the team's acceptance tests (`StringCalculatorAcceptance`). Press it after every red and every green: the rows are your TDD loop.
starter: public static int Add(string numbers) => throw new NotImplementedException();
solution: if (negatives.Count > 0) throw new ArgumentException("negatives not allowed: " + string.Join(", ", negatives));
public void Adds_comma_separated_numbers(string input, int expected) => Assert.Equal(expected, StringCalculator.Add(input));
public void Numbers_above_1000_are_ignored(string input, int expected) => Assert.Equal(expected, StringCalculator.Add(input));
template: public void Adds(string input, int expected) => Assert.Equal(expected, StringCalculator.Add(input));
hints: Go in order. After `""` and one number, `numbers.Split(',').Sum(int.Parse)` handles any amount.
For the custom separator: if the text starts with `//`, the separator is between index 2 and the first `\n`, and the numbers start after it. `Split` accepts an array of string separators.
Collect the negatives with `Where(v => v < 0)` before summing, and throw `new ArgumentException("negatives not allowed: " + string.Join(", ", negatives))`.
steps.explain: Each requirement arrived as a failing test, so every branch in the code has a test that demands it. The acceptance tests passing on the first try is the payoff of working down your own list.
